question.text: If an exporter uses USDINR futures to hedge and INR appreciates, what happens?

answer.text: Exporter receives less INR on spot conversion but gains on the short futures position — net effect is approximately the locked-in rate
Exporter loses on both spot conversion and futures
Exporter receives more INR on spot conversion and also gains on futures

explanation.text: The Logic: In the INR-appreciation case, the exporter receives Re. 1 less than budget on spot conversion but gains Rs. 1.70 on the sold futures contract, leaving an effective rate of Rs. 81.70 — futures lock in the price irrespective of INR depreciation or appreciation. The Trap: The hedge works in BOTH directions — it prevents losses but also limits windfall gains. The workbook compares the hedged rate of Rs. 81.70 versus unhedged rates of Rs. 83 and Rs. 80. Note: This is the fundamental trade-off of hedging: certainty of rate vs. giving up potential favorable movements. Source: NISM-Series-I Currency Derivatives workbook, pp.97-98.
